Edgar W. Jenkins and N. W. Nelson

📚 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐠𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐬𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐠𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐞𝐞 𝐢𝐭 𝐚𝐬 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐟𝐮𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬?

In this 2005 article, Jenkins and Nelson examined responses from 1,266 students in England, drawing on the international Relevance of Science Education (ROSE) project. Their findings revealed a striking contrast: 68% agreed that everyone should learn science at school, and 61% found it interesting, yet only 21% wanted to become scientists. Significant differences also emerged between girls' and boys' experiences of science and their interests in particular topics.

At a time when international assessments increasingly emphasised achievement, the article helped bring students' perspectives into conversations about science curriculum reform. Its contribution went beyond documenting attitudes: it questioned whose understanding of relevance should shape school science.

More than two decades later, scientific technologies, career opportunities and educational priorities have evolved. Yet the questions raised by this study remain pertinent. Why might students value science without wanting to pursue it? How can science curricula respond to students' interests while ensuring broad and equitable learning opportunities?

Revisiting this paper invites us to reflect on what has changed since 2005—and what remains unresolved in making school science meaningful to young people.

Read the article: https://doi.org/10.1080/02635140500068435
